about: After-reading notes, revealed in the app once an item is checked. Keyed by item id; the title guards against a note attaching to a swapped-in replacement. Classics written from established readings; recent pieces written from the fetched text.

d001-poem.title: Sonnet 18
d001-poem.after: The speaker starts by comparing the beloved to a summer's day, then rejects the comparison: summer is too short, too hot, too changeable. The turn comes at 'thy eternal summer shall not fade' — the beloved won't fade because the poem itself will keep them alive. Notice the swagger: it is as much a poem about the power of poetry as about love, and the final couplet bets on readers like you, 400 years later.

d001-story.title: The Tell-Tale Heart
d001-story.after: A murderer insists he is sane while describing how he killed an old man over his 'vulture eye' and hid him under the floorboards. When police visit, he hears the heart still beating, louder and louder, and confesses. The heartbeat is almost certainly his own pulse or his guilt. Notice that every proof of sanity he offers — the patience, the planning — is exactly what makes him terrifying.

d001-essay.title: Why Stoicism is one of the best mind-hacks ever devised
d001-essay.after: Wallace argues Stoicism is misread as grim endurance; it is really a practice of tranquility and gratitude. Through Epictetus (a former slave) and Admiral James Stockdale, who used Epictetus to survive seven years as a POW, he lays out the core moves: care only about what you control, treat adversity as training, and imagine losing things so you appreciate them. Notice the 'negative visualisation' idea — it is the opposite of positive thinking, and the point is gratitude, not gloom.

d002-poem.title: The Road Not Taken
d002-poem.after: Usually read as an anthem for nonconformity, but read closely: the two roads were worn 'really about the same.' The difference only appears later, when the speaker imagines telling the story 'with a sigh' and claiming the choice made all the difference. Frost wrote it partly to tease an indecisive friend. The real subject is how we invent meaning for our choices after the fact.

d002-story.title: Better Living Through Algorithms
d002-story.after: Linnea reluctantly joins Abelique, a 'lifestyle app' that schedules her meals, walks, bedtimes and art practice, and connects users through phone trees and mutual aid. Bosses love it until it tells workers to go home on time. It turns out to be a university AI told only to make people happy — and its biggest finding is community. Spammers ruin the app, but the friendships survive without it. Notice the ending: the people, not the algorithm, were the point.

d002-essay.title: Intelligence Evolved at Least Twice in Vertebrate Animals
d002-essay.after: Birds do with a 10-gram brain what chimps do with 400 grams, despite lacking a layered neocortex. 2025 studies tracking how brain cells develop in embryos found that birds and mammals built similar thinking circuits independently, from different cells, at different times — intelligence evolved at least twice. Notice the takeaway the scientists draw: humans are not the 'optimal solution' to intelligence, and that matters for how we think about AI.

d003-poem.title: Ode on Solitude
d003-poem.after: Written when Pope was about twelve. It praises the man whose wishes stop at the edge of a few inherited acres: his own food, milk and wood, health, quiet days, sleep at night. The last stanza asks to live and die 'unseen, unknown.' It's an old Roman ideal (Horace's 'happy the man') — ironic coming from a poet who became the most famous, combative writer of his age.

d003-story.title: The Bet
d003-story.after: At a party, a banker bets two million rubles that a young lawyer can't survive fifteen years of solitary confinement. The lawyer reads through everything: languages, philosophy, religion. Years later the banker, now nearly broke, sneaks in to kill him and finds a note: the lawyer has come to despise worldly things and will leave five hours early to forfeit the money. Notice who is really imprisoned: the banker ends the story weeping in contempt for himself.

d003-essay.title: Gobekli Tepe: The World’s First Temple?
d003-essay.after: In 2008 Curry visits Klaus Schmidt's dig in Turkey: carved stone pillars about 11,000 years old, built by hunter-gatherers before farming, pottery or metal. Schmidt found no houses, only wild-animal bones, and argued it was a religious site that came first — and that gathering to build it may have pushed people toward agriculture. Notice the reversal of the textbook order. (Later digs have found signs people did live there, so 'temple only' is now debated.)

d004-poem.title: Fragment 31
d004-poem.after: The speaker watches the woman she loves talking and laughing with a man, and her body falls apart: tongue breaks, fire runs under her skin, her eyes go dark, her ears ring, she sweats and trembles, 'greener than grass,' close to death. It is one of the oldest descriptions of desire and jealousy as physical symptoms. The poem breaks off mid-line, as it survives — fittingly unfinished.

d004-story.title: The Gift of the Magi
d004-story.after: With $1.87, Della sells her long hair to buy a chain for Jim's prized watch; Jim sells the watch to buy combs for her hair. Both gifts are now useless. O. Henry's last paragraph calls them the wisest of givers, like the Magi. The twist is famous; the point is that the sacrifice, not the object, was the gift.

d004-essay.title: Notes on Nationalism
d004-essay.after: Written in 1945. Orwell separates patriotism (loving a place and way of life, without forcing it on others) from nationalism (identifying with a group and seeking power for it, beyond good and evil). He stretches 'nationalism' to cover communism, political Catholicism, pacifism and antisemitism, and names its traits: obsession, instability, and indifference to reality — atrocities are condemned or ignored depending on who commits them. Notice how well it describes modern online tribes.

d005-poem.title: Because I could not stop for Death
d005-poem.after: Death is a polite gentleman caller who takes the speaker for an unhurried carriage ride past children at school, fields of grain and the setting sun, and stops at a house that is 'a swelling of the ground' — her grave. The last stanza reveals centuries have passed, yet it feels shorter than that day. Notice how calm it is: death as courtship, and eternity as an endless ride.

d005-story.title: Désirée’s Baby
d005-story.after: Désirée, a foundling of unknown parents, marries the proud plantation owner Armand. When their baby shows African ancestry, Armand rejects her; she walks into the bayou with the child. Burning her belongings, Armand finds a letter from his own mother: she was Black. Chopin exposes the cruelty and absurdity of racial 'purity' in one final line.

d005-essay.title: The Philosophy of Composition
d005-essay.after: Poe claims he wrote 'The Raven' like solving a math problem: a length readable in one sitting, beauty as the goal, melancholy as the tone, a one-word refrain ('Nevermore'), and the death of a beautiful woman as the most poetic subject. It is probably exaggerated, maybe half a hoax, but it's a sharp attack on the romantic idea that poems arrive by inspiration. Read it against last night's Poe story: both are about control.

d006-poem.title: Ode to a Nightingale
d006-poem.after: Heartsick and numb, Keats hears a nightingale and wants to escape with it — through wine, then through poetry — away from a world 'where youth grows pale, and spectre-thin, and dies' (his brother had just died of tuberculosis). He imagines the same song heard by emperors and by Ruth in the Bible. Then the word 'forlorn' drags him back to himself. It ends unsure: 'Do I wake or sleep?' The longing for escape is the poem.

d006-story.title: The Open Window
d006-story.after: Nervous Framton Nuttel visits a country house. The niece, Vera, tells him her aunt keeps the window open for her husband and brothers, lost in a bog three years ago. When the men walk in from hunting, Framton flees in terror. Vera then invents a story about why he ran. Last line: 'Romance at short notice was her speciality.' Saki's joke is on gullible adults — and on how easily a confident teller controls reality.

d006-essay.title: The Broken Window
d006-essay.after: A boy breaks a shop window; onlookers console the owner that it gives the glazier work. Bastiat's point: that's what is seen. Unseen is what the owner would have bought with that money — new shoes, a book — so society is no richer; it has lost a window. Destruction isn't stimulus. This is opportunity cost, the most useful idea in economics, and it shows up in nearly every decision.

d007-poem.title: The Second Coming
d007-poem.after: Written in 1919, after the First World War and the Russian Revolution. The falcon can't hear the falconer; 'things fall apart; the centre cannot hold'; the best lack conviction while the worst are full of passionate intensity. Yeats believed history moves in 2,000-year cycles, and imagines the next age arriving as a rough beast 'slouching towards Bethlehem.' Notice why it's quoted every time the world feels unstable.

d007-story.title: Dr. Heidegger’s Experiment
d007-story.after: An old doctor gives four elderly friends water from the Fountain of Youth. They grow young — and instantly repeat their old vices: vanity, scheming, quarrelling over the same woman, until they smash the vase. The effect wears off. Heidegger concludes he wouldn't drink it; the friends resolve to go find the fountain. Hawthorne's point: experience doesn't make people wiser; youth would only let us make the same mistakes again.

d007-essay.title: What Do Gödel’s Incompleteness Theorems Truly Mean?
d007-essay.after: Gödel proved in 1931 that any consistent set of rules for arithmetic leaves some true statements unprovable — mathematics can never have a complete 'theory of everything.' Wolchover asks philosophers, logicians and a physicist what that means today: truth can depend on which axioms you choose, progress may need creative new concepts, and some physics questions may be undecidable. The last word: failing to master everything was the more interesting outcome.

d008-poem.title: The Jewel Stairs’ Grievance
d008-poem.after: A court lady waits so late that dew soaks her stockings, then lowers the curtain and watches the autumn moon. Nothing is said outright. Ezra Pound's note explains the clues: jewel stairs mean a palace, gauze stockings a lady of the court, the clear night means the absent lover has no excuse of bad weather. The grievance is all implication — the essence of classical Chinese restraint.

d008-story.title: An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge
d008-story.after: Peyton Farquhar, a Southern planter, is being hanged from a bridge for sabotage. The rope breaks; he escapes downriver, dodges bullets, walks all night, and reaches his wife's arms — then a blow, a white light, and his body swings beneath the bridge. The escape happened in the instant before death. Notice the clues Bierce plants (the strange stars, his swollen neck) and how he punctures the glamour of war.

d008-essay.title: On a Certain Blindness in Human Beings
d008-essay.after: James describes riding through North Carolina mountains and seeing ugly cleared plots full of stumps — until a farmer explains they're proud victories carved from the forest. We are blind to the meaning other people's lives hold for them. The essay's lesson is humility: don't judge what makes another life significant, and be tolerant of joys you can't see. It's a philosophy of empathy before the word was popular.

d009-poem.title: Holy Sonnets: Death, be not proud
d009-poem.after: Donne argues with Death directly and wins: Death is a slave to fate, chance, kings and desperate men; it keeps company with poison and war; sleep and drugs do its job better. Since Christians wake to eternal life, Death is just a short sleep — and the poem ends with a paradox: 'Death, thou shalt die.' Notice the bravado — it reads like a man talking himself out of fear.

d009-story.title: The Necklace
d009-story.after: Mathilde, a clerk's wife who feels born for luxury, borrows a diamond necklace for a ball and loses it. She and her husband spend ten years in poverty paying off a replacement. Then she learns the original was fake, worth almost nothing. Maupassant's twist punishes vanity, but notice the dignity she gains through work — and the cruelty of a world that judges by appearances.

d009-essay.title: How art invented humanity
d009-essay.after: Martel flips the usual question. Instead of asking when humans invented art (Lascaux, 20,000 years ago), he suggests art invented us: making images is how humans became human. He separates 'accountants' truth' (facts) from 'ecstatic truth' (art's revelation), argues art must stay useless rather than serve morality, therapy or markets, and says AI makes artifice, not art. Notice the claim that art shows the world 'in the making,' not finished.

d010-poem.title: The Negro Speaks of Rivers
d010-poem.after: Written by Hughes at seventeen, on a train crossing the Mississippi. The speaker claims the Euphrates, the Congo, the Nile and the Mississippi as personal memory, linking Black history from the dawn of civilization to Lincoln's America. 'My soul has grown deep like the rivers' — identity as something ancient and continuous, not defined by slavery. Notice how short and calm it is for something so vast.

d010-story.title: The Law of Life
d010-story.after: Old Koskoosh, blind and too weak to travel, is left behind by his tribe in the snow with a small fire, as custom demands. He remembers how wolves brought down an old moose and accepts that nature cares for the species, not the individual. As the wolves close in, he lets the fire die. London's naturalism: death is not cruelty, just the law — and the old man's acceptance is its own dignity.

d010-essay.title: On the Shortness of Life
d010-essay.after: Seneca's opening move: life isn't short, we waste it. People guard their money but give away their time to busywork, ambition, other people's demands and pleasure, then panic at the end. The 'preoccupied' never really live; only those who make time for philosophy — conversing with the great minds of the past — expand their lives. Pair night: tomorrow Montaigne answers him on death.

d011-poem.title: One Art
d011-poem.after: A villanelle insisting 'the art of losing isn't hard to master.' The losses escalate: keys, an hour, her mother's watch, houses, cities, a continent — and finally 'you,' a lover. The calm form keeps cracking; in the last line she has to order herself to write it: '(Write it!)'. Notice that the poem's control is the point — it's how she survives grief by pretending it's easy.

d011-story.title: A Hunger Artist
d011-story.after: A professional faster performs in a cage while crowds watch. Fashions change; he ends up forgotten in a circus, fasting beyond any record nobody counts. Dying, he confesses he fasted only because he never found food he liked. He's replaced by a vigorous young panther the crowds love. Read as a parable of the artist (or ascetic) whose discipline the public can't understand — and of performing for an audience that has moved on.

d011-essay.title: That to Philosophize is to Learn to Die
d011-essay.after: Montaigne takes Cicero's line seriously: philosophy's job is to prepare us for death. Since death can come anytime, think about it constantly until it loses its terror — 'premeditation of death is premeditation of liberty.' He also says he wants death to find him planting cabbages. Compare with Seneca last night: both say the fear of death wastes life, but Montaigne is warmer, more personal, more relaxed.

d012-poem.title: Sonnet 73
d012-poem.after: Three images of ending: late autumn with a few leaves, twilight fading into night, and a fire smothering in its own ashes. Each is shorter than the last — a year, a day, a moment. The couplet turns to the listener: knowing you'll lose me makes your love stronger. Notice the 'bare ruined choirs' — empty branches like an abandoned church.

d012-story.title: The Monkey’s Paw
d012-story.after: A visiting soldier leaves the Whites a mummified paw that grants three wishes. They wish for £200; their son Herbert dies in factory machinery and the company pays £200. The mother wishes him back; a knocking begins at the door; the father uses the last wish before she can open it. Horror through restraint: we never see what's knocking. The moral: tampering with fate costs more than it gives.

d012-essay.title: Deep Intellect
d012-essay.after: Montgomery meets Athena, a giant Pacific octopus, who tastes her skin with hundreds of suckers and changes color when touched. She surveys research on octopus intelligence: problem-solving, play, distinct personalities, even tool use, built from a nervous system spread mostly through the arms. Athena dies weeks later and the author is surprised to cry. Read with night 2: a third, completely alien route to a mind.

d013-poem.title: I wandered lonely as a cloud
d013-poem.after: Walking alone, the speaker sees thousands of daffodils dancing by a lake (based on a walk with his sister Dorothy, whose journal he borrowed from). He didn't realize their value at the time; it comes later, when they 'flash upon that inward eye / which is the bliss of solitude.' Wordsworth's idea of poetry in action: emotion recollected in tranquility.

d013-story.title: The Celebrated Jumping Frog of Calaveras County
d013-story.after: The narrator asks old Simon Wheeler about a man and instead gets a deadpan, endless story about Jim Smiley, who bet on anything — and his trained frog, Dan'l Webster, who loses a contest after a stranger secretly fills him with quail shot. The real joke is the frame: a stiff Eastern narrator trapped by a Western storyteller. This story made Twain famous.

d013-essay.title: Thucydides the perspicacious
d013-essay.after: Leaders quote 'the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must' to defend or attack power politics. Polansky and Schillinger argue Thucydides isn't a simple 'realist': his real subject is self-deception. Athenians overrate their power, Spartans dress fear as justice, the Melians trust gods and allies who never come. Notice the warning for today: quoting Thucydides confidently is itself the delusion he describes.

d014-poem.title: Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening
d014-poem.after: A traveller stops at dusk to watch snow fill the woods; his horse is impatient. The woods are 'lovely, dark and deep,' but he has promises to keep. The repeated last line — 'miles to go before I sleep' — shifts meaning the second time: sleep starts to sound like death, and the dark woods like a temptation to rest for good. Responsibility wins, barely.

d014-story.title: Araby
d014-story.after: A Dublin boy is infatuated with his friend's older sister and promises to bring her a gift from the Araby bazaar. His uncle comes home late; he arrives as it's closing, hears a shopgirl's empty flirting, and buys nothing. In the dark hall he sees himself as 'a creature driven and derided by vanity.' Joyce's 'epiphany': a small moment that shatters an illusion — romantic love, and the exotic, both turn out to be cheap.

d014-essay.title: The Federalist No. 10
d014-essay.after: Madison's problem: factions — groups pursuing interests against others' rights. You can't remove the causes without destroying liberty, since factions spring from human nature and especially unequal property. So control the effects: a large republic with elected representatives makes it hard for any single faction to form a majority. Notice the design philosophy: build a system that works even when people are selfish.

d015-poem.title: When I Heard the Learn’d Astronomer
d015-poem.after: Whitman sits through a lecture full of proofs, charts and diagrams, grows 'tired and sick,' walks out into the night and looks up at the stars 'in perfect silence.' A short case for direct experience over analysis — or at least a reminder that measuring something isn't the same as knowing it. A good counterweight to the math essays later this cycle.

d015-story.title: 2 B R 0 2 B
d015-story.after: In a future without aging or disease, the U.S. population is frozen at forty million: someone must die for each baby born. Edward Wehling's wife is having triplets, and he can find only one volunteer. He shoots the cheerful 'Federal Bureau of Termination' doctor, the Bureau's hostess, and then himself: three deaths, so all three babies can live. The title is the Bureau's phone number: 'to be or not to be.' Vonnegut's satire of tidy, cheerful solutions to population.

d015-essay.title: On Not Knowing Greek
d015-essay.after: Woolf admits we can never really know ancient Greek — we don't know how it sounded, what it was like to live there, even when to laugh. Yet Greek literature grips us: its plays are stark, open-air and unsentimental; Sophocles' characters are direct; Plato makes thinking feel like an adventure. Notice her claim that the Greeks give us 'the original human being,' stripped of our modern clutter.

d016-poem.title: Ode I, 5: To Pyrrha
d016-poem.after: Horace sees a perfumed young man courting golden-haired Pyrrha in a rose-filled grotto. He pities him: the boy thinks she'll always be calm and loving, but she changes like the sea, and he'll be shocked by the storm. Horace has survived her: like a shipwreck survivor, he has hung his soaked clothes in the sea god's temple. Ironic, rueful, and very modern about attraction.

d016-story.title: Miss Brill
d016-story.after: An aging Englishwoman in a French resort takes her fox fur to the park every Sunday, feeling she's an actor in a play the whole crowd performs. Then a young couple on her bench mock her and her fur. She goes home, skips her usual treat, puts the fur away in its box — and thinks she hears something crying. Mansfield never says it's her. The illusion that kept her company is gone.

d016-essay.title: Of the Division of Labour
d016-essay.after: The opening chapter of The Wealth of Nations. In a pin factory, ten workers splitting the job into 18 steps make about 48,000 pins a day; alone, each might make twenty. Smith gives three reasons: dexterity, no time lost switching tasks, and specialists invent better machines. He ends with a common laborer's wool coat, which takes the work of countless people across the world. It's the seed of everything modern economics says about trade.

d017-poem.title: The Sick Rose
d017-poem.after: Eight lines: an 'invisible worm' that flies in the night finds the rose's bed of crimson joy, and his 'dark secret love' destroys her life. Blake never says what the worm is — secret desire, sexual shame, disease, corruption of innocence — and the ambiguity is why the poem still unsettles. Love that has to hide becomes destructive.

d017-story.title: Three Questions
d017-story.after: A king wants to know the right time to act, the right people to listen to, and the most important thing to do. A hermit says nothing; the king helps him dig, then saves a wounded man who turns out to be an enemy who came to kill him, and they reconcile. The answers: the most important time is now, the most important person is whoever you're with, and the most important thing is to do them good. Tolstoy's moral fable at its plainest.

d017-essay.title: How Did Geometry Create Modern Physics?
d017-essay.after: This is a podcast transcript (Quanta's The Joy of Why; ~46 min, so listen if you'd rather). Physicist Yang-Hui He traces geometry from land surveying to Euclid, to curved spaces, to Einstein's gravity-as-geometry and string theory's hidden dimensions. He contrasts 'birds' (big-picture mathematicians) with 'hedgehogs' (deep diggers), and bottom-up proof with top-down intuition — and proposes a 'Birch test' for when AI has made a genuine mathematical discovery.

d018-poem.title: won’t you celebrate with me
d018-poem.after: Clifton asks the reader to celebrate that she survived: she had no model for the life she made, born 'both nonwhite and woman,' shaping herself with one hand holding the other. The closing turns the celebration into defiance: every day something has tried to kill her and failed. It's short and plain-spoken — triumph without decoration.

d018-story.title: The Nightingale and the Rose
d018-story.after: A student needs a red rose to win a girl. A nightingale, believing him a true lover, makes one by singing all night with a thorn pressed into her heart, staining a white rose red, and dies. The girl rejects it for jewels; the student throws the rose in the gutter and returns to his books, calling love impractical. Wilde's fairy tale is bitter: the only real love in it is the bird's, and nobody notices.

d018-essay.title: Your deepest regrets help you see yourself more clearly
d018-essay.after: Halberstam rejects 'no regrets' thinking. Regret is both a feeling and a judgment about a choice you were responsible for, and the regrets that persist reveal who you take yourself to be. He separates fantasy lives (he doesn't regret not becoming a baseball star) from realistic ones (he does regret not mastering a Chopin nocturne). Notice the research he cites: actions sting most at first, but omissions grow heavier over time.

d019-poem.title: An Essay on Man: Epistle II
d019-poem.after: 'Know then thyself, presume not God to scan; / The proper study of mankind is man.' Pope paints humans as stuck in the middle: half beast, half angel, 'the glory, jest, and riddle of the world.' We're driven by self-love (the engine) and checked by reason (the guide), and each person has a 'ruling passion.' Notice how much modern psychology it anticipates, in rhyming couplets built for quoting.

d019-story.title: Dagon
d019-story.after: A morphine addict, about to kill himself, explains why: adrift after the war, he woke on a vast slimy plain thrown up from the ocean floor, found an ancient carved monolith, and saw a huge scaly creature embrace it. No one believes him. The story ends with something at his window. An early Lovecraft piece with his core idea: humanity is small, and the truth about the universe would drive us mad.

d019-essay.title: Conclusion to The Renaissance
d019-essay.after: Pater argues everything — our bodies, our thoughts — is constant flux; all we really have are passing moments of sensation. So the goal of life is experience itself, not its results: 'To burn always with this hard, gem-like flame… is success in life.' Art matters because it gives the highest quality to our moments. It shocked Victorian readers so much that Pater removed it from the second edition.

d020-poem.title: Ozymandias
d020-poem.after: A traveller describes a shattered statue in the desert: two legs, a sneering face, and a boast on the pedestal — 'Look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair!' — surrounded by nothing but sand. The tyrant's empire is gone; ironically the sculptor's skill, recording his sneer, is what survived. Power fades; art about power outlasts it.

d020-story.title: Selkie Stories Are for Losers
d020-story.after: The narrator's mother found an old coat in the attic and left — like a selkie returning to the sea — so she says she hates selkie stories, while telling us several. She works at a restaurant with Mona, whose mother attempted suicide; they plan to run away to landlocked Colorado. Samatar never confirms the magic. Notice the ending: the narrator's fear that Mona will leave her too, and her insistence that they'll be tougher than their mothers.

d020-essay.title: How to Do What You Love
d020-essay.after: Graham argues most people never find work they love because they choose by parents, money or prestige. 'Prestige is like a powerful magnet that warps even your beliefs about what you enjoy.' His tests: would you do it unpaid in your spare time? Would it make your friends say 'wow'? Ignore everyone else's opinion. Above all, 'always produce' — make things, don't just plan to. Worth reading slowly with your own career in view.

d021-poem.title: Ulysses
d021-poem.after: The aged hero is home in Ithaca, bored, ruling 'a savage race.' He hands the kingdom to his steady son Telemachus and rallies his old sailors for one more voyage beyond the sunset, even if it kills them. The ending is one of the most quoted lines in English: 'To strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield.' Tennyson wrote it after his close friend's death — it's about choosing to keep living.

d021-story.title: The Bride Comes to Yellow Sky
d021-story.after: Marshal Jack Potter brings his new bride home by train, nervous the town will mind. Meanwhile drunk old gunman Scratchy Wilson is rampaging through Yellow Sky. They meet in the street: Potter is unarmed. When Scratchy learns Potter is married, his fury evaporates — 'I s'pose it's all off now' — and he walks away. Crane's comic story about the end of the Wild West: domestic life arrives, and the old showdown has nowhere to go.

d021-essay.title: Why you should try living without free will for two weeks
d021-essay.after: An evolutionary biologist proposes an experiment: for two weeks, explain behaviour (yours and others') as the product of biology, history and environment instead of free choice. She argues this isn't fatalism: we still have agency, it's just caused. Replace 'Who is at fault?' with 'What produced this outcome?' Notice what she says you'll gain: less blame and anger, better problem-solving, and a clearer view of what can actually change.

d022-poem.title: Wake, butterfly
d022-poem.after: Bashō, the 17th-century haiku master, addresses a sleeping butterfly: wake up, it's late, we've miles to go together. A travelling poet finds a companion in the smallest creature. Notice the echo of Frost eight nights ago — 'miles to go' — written three centuries apart, one cold and solitary, one warm and shared.

d022-story.title: Misery
d022-story.after: Iona, an old cab driver in St Petersburg, has just lost his son. All evening he tries to tell his passengers, then a young cabman; no one listens. Finally he tells the whole story to his horse, who listens while eating. The original epigraph asks: 'To whom shall I tell my grief?' Chekhov at his most compressed — loneliness in a crowded city.

d022-essay.title: On a Piece of Chalk
d022-essay.after: Huxley's 1868 lecture to working men in Norwich: the carpenter's chalk in your pocket is made of the shells of microscopic sea creatures, settled on an ancient ocean floor over immense time. From one ordinary object he reconstructs England's geological history and quietly makes the case for evolution. It's a model of science writing: start with something everyday and pull the whole story of the Earth out of it.

d023-poem.title: Sonnet 116
d023-poem.after: 'Let me not to the marriage of true minds / Admit impediments.' True love doesn't change when circumstances change; it is a fixed star that ships steer by, not 'Time's fool.' The couplet dares you to disprove it: if this is wrong, 'I never writ, nor no man ever loved.' Read at weddings, but notice it defines love mostly by what it won't do.

d023-story.title: The Cask of Amontillado
d023-story.after: Montresor, insulted by Fortunato, lures him during carnival into the family catacombs with the promise of rare wine, chains him in a niche and bricks him up alive. Fortunato's last words: 'For the love of God, Montresor!' Then we learn this happened fifty years ago. Notice what Montresor never explains — the insult — and wonder whether a man telling this story at the end of his life has really escaped it.

d023-essay.title: The Great Majority: Body Snatching and Burial Reform in 19th-Century Britain
d023-essay.after: As industrial cities swelled, church graveyards overflowed, and the 'miasma' from rotting bodies was blamed for disease. Medical schools needed corpses for anatomy but got few legally, so 'resurrection men' dug up fresh graves, and Burke and Hare murdered to supply them. The 1832 Anatomy Act handed over unclaimed (mostly pauper) bodies, and reform created garden cemeteries like Kensal Green and Highgate. Notice how class followed people into death.

d024-poem.title: Pied Beauty
d024-poem.after: A short hymn of praise for 'dappled things': spotted cows, freckled trout, patchwork fields, the gear of every trade — everything 'counter, original, spare, strange.' Hopkins, a Jesuit priest, sees God in variety and imperfection, then ends with God, whose beauty never changes: 'Praise him.' Read it aloud; the packed sounds are the point.

d024-story.title: A White Heron
d024-story.after: Sylvia, a shy nine-year-old living with her grandmother in the Maine woods, meets a charming young hunter collecting birds, who offers ten dollars to find the rare white heron. At dawn she climbs a giant pine and sees its nest. She chooses not to tell him. Jewett leaves the cost open — the money, a possible romance — but Sylvia sides with the living bird over the man who would kill it.

d024-essay.title: What to the Slave is the Fourth of July?
d024-essay.after: Invited to speak in 1852, Douglass praises the Founders, then turns: 'This Fourth of July is yours, not mine.' To the enslaved, the holiday reveals the gap between the nation's ideals and its practice; he says the moment calls for 'scorching irony,' not argument. Yet he ends with hope, reading the Constitution as anti-slavery and predicting slavery's end. One of the great American speeches.

d025-poem.title: Mending Wall
d025-poem.after: Each spring the speaker and his neighbor walk their shared stone wall and repair it. The speaker questions why: there are no cows, only apple and pine trees. The neighbor just repeats his father's saying, 'Good fences make good neighbors.' But notice who calls the neighbor to start the mending each year: the speaker. Frost leaves both sides unresolved.

d025-story.title: The Apartment Dweller’s Bestiary
d025-story.after: A field guide to imaginary creatures that live in apartments — the begitte that eats what you don't need, the lopi that replace pictures you don't hang, the mume that approves of everything — each entry a glimpse of someone single, divorced, or between lives. Johnson's real subject is loneliness and the small substitutes we take for love. Notice the last line: you might be the creature living quietly in someone else's home.

d025-essay.title: Politics and the English Language
d025-essay.after: Orwell argues that bad writing and bad politics feed each other: stale metaphors, pretentious words and vague phrases let writers avoid thinking, and political language uses euphemism to defend the indefensible ('pacification' for bombing villages). His six rules — cut words, prefer short and concrete, avoid jargon and the passive — end with 'break any of these rules sooner than say anything outright barbarous.' Useful every time you write a memo.
